requests.question: How do our separate General chapters 13 and 14 on oxytocin/OXTR, IL-6 and mental health differ? Give both exact chapter titles and source counts, then explain their focus in under 170 words.

response.answer:
- **General chapter 13: “Oxytocin, OXTR and IL-6” — 42 sources.** [S1]
- **General chapter 14: “IL-6 and mental health” — 120 peer-reviewed publications:** 117 directly relevant mental-health papers and three contextual exposure papers. [S2]

**Chapter 13 is pathway-focused:** how oxytocin and its receptor, OXTR, affect IL-6 and other inflammation markers in cells, animals and humans. Selected laboratory models show strong effects, alongside null and opposite-direction results. Human findings are promising but mixed; sustained anti-inflammatory benefit is not established. [S1]

**Chapter 14 is condition-focused:** IL-6 associations and intervention evidence across depression, schizophrenia/psychosis, bipolar depression, mania, hypomania, anxiety, PTSD, suicidality, ADHD and substance use disorders. It distinguishes association, biomarker change and clinical benefit, retaining diagnosis-specific gaps. IL-6 is not established as a universal cause of mental illness. [S2]

These are separate, complementary chapters. Linking OXTR interventions to mental-health improvement through IL-6 remains a hypothesis. Source counts are not independent-study counts. [S1][S2]

requests.question: In our separate IL-6 and mental health chapter, what does the ADHD evidence show? Contrast positive and null trials and pooled evidence. Keep it under 170 words.

response.answer:
Chapter 14’s **ADHD evidence is mixed**. [S1]

- **Positive trial:** An eight-week adjunctive omega-3 randomized trial (103 children) reported lower IL-6 and improved parent-rated symptoms. Parallel changes do not prove that IL-6 reduction caused improvement. [S2]
- **Null/non-specific trials:** Vitamin D did not significantly reduce IL-6 versus placebo after three months. [S3] In a probiotic pilot, IL-6 fell in both groups—not evidence of a probiotic-specific effect—despite improved child-reported quality of life. [S4]
- **Pooled evidence:** A 2021 meta-analysis found no significant IL-6 difference (p=0.09), with few cytokine studies. [S5] A 2022 analysis found higher IL-6, but significance disappeared when individual studies were removed. [S6] A 2026 network meta-analysis highlighted elevated IL-6 in autism; that finding cannot be transferred to ADHD. [S7]

Limited, heterogeneous evidence and abstract-based omega-3/pooled appraisals constrain certainty. Neither IL-6 as a routine ADHD treatment target nor an OXTR mechanism is established. [S1]

sources.label: S2
sources.title: Effect of n-3 supplementation on hyperactivity, oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators in children with attention-deficit-hyperactivity disorder.
sources.authors: Hariri M, Djazayery A, Djalali M, Saedisomeolia A, Rahimi A, Abdolahian E.
sources.text: Eight weeks of EPA/DHA added to maintenance treatment reduced IL-6 and CRP and improved parent-rated symptoms in the reported study.

sources.label: S3
sources.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on Inflammatory Biomarkers in School-Aged Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.
sources.authors: Samadi M, Gholami F, Seyedi M, Jalali M, Effatpanah M, Yekaninejad MS, Abdolahi M, Chamari M, Mohammadzadeh Honarvar N.
sources.text: Vitamin D increased circulating vitamin D but did not significantly reduce IL-6 or TNF compared with placebo after three months.

sources.label: S4
sources.title: A Pilot Randomized Control Trial With the Probiotic Strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) in ADHD: Children and Adolescents Report Better Health-Related Quality of Life.
sources.authors: Kumperscak HG, Gricar A, Ülen I, Micetic-Turk D.
sources.text: Probiotic supplementation improved child-reported quality of life, while parent/teacher findings were less consistent. IL-6 decreased in both probiotic and placebo groups.

sources.label: S5
sources.title: Cortisol and inflammatory biomarker levels in youths with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): evidence from a systematic review with meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Chang JP, Su KP, Mondelli V, Pariante CM.
sources.text: The pooled inflammatory evidence did not show a significant IL-6 difference (p=0.09), despite a lower TNF signal. Most studies in the broader review concerned cortisol, not cytokines.

sources.label: S6
sources.title: Peripheral blood inflammatory markers in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Misiak B, Wójta-Kempa M, Samochowiec J, Schiweck C, Aichholzer M, Reif A, Samochowiec A, Stańczykiewicz B.
sources.text: ADHD was associated with higher peripheral IL-6 (pooled g about 0.7), but removal of individual studies made the pooled result nonsignificant. Other cytokines had different or absent associations.

sources.label: S7
sources.title: Inflammatory cytokine alterations in autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Chen Q, Sun Y, Pan N, Long Y, Cao Y, Luo Y, Xin K, Chen P, Wang Y, Shu M, Chen Y, Gong Q.
sources.text: The analysis found distinct immune patterns: elevated IL-6 was highlighted for autism, while ADHD findings centred on lower TNF, IL-2 and MCP-1.
